title: Jainendra Jain Becomes First Indian-Origin Physicist to Win Wolf Prize
excerpt: The Penn State professor and Rajasthan native received the 2025 Wolf Prize in Physics for his discovery of composite fermions, a breakthrough central to quantum computing research.
body:
• Jainendra K. Jain received the 2025 Wolf Prize in Physics at a ceremony in Jerusalem on June 18, becoming the first person of Indian origin to win the award in physics.
  • His 1989 discovery of composite fermions provided a unified explanation of the fractional quantum Hall effect, reshaping condensed matter physics.
  • Twenty-seven previous Wolf Prize Physics recipients have gone on to win the Nobel Prize, placing Jain among the field's most elite researchers.
  • Jain grew up in rural Rajasthan and overcame a childhood accident that left him with a lifelong disability, crediting the Jaipur Foot prosthetic with enabling his education.

Indian American physicist Jainendra K. Jain has won the 2025 Wolf Prize in Physics for his discovery of composite fermions, a class of particles that transformed the understanding of quantum matter. Israeli President Isaac Herzog presented the award at a state ceremony in the Knesset on June 18, 2026.

Jain, who serves as Evan Pugh University Professor and Eberly Family Chair in Physics at Pennsylvania State University, shares the prize with experimentalists James P. Eisenstein and Mordehai Heiblum. He is the first person of Indian origin to receive the Wolf Prize in Physics.

A Discovery Born During a Commercial Break

The breakthrough that earned Jain global recognition came in 1989, when he was a postdoctoral researcher at Yale University. Working on the fractional quantum Hall effect — a phenomenon where electrons in ultra-thin semiconductor layers under powerful magnetic fields exhibit baffling behavior — Jain realized that electrons could bind to tiny quanta of magnetic field to form entirely new particles.

"The key insight is that electrons can bind to tiny quanta of magnetic field to form entirely new particles called composite fermions, which, remarkably, interact only weakly."

— Jainendra K. Jain, Wolf Prize Laureate

He named these particles composite fermions. The idea came to him, he has recounted, while doodling during a television commercial break. Published in Physical Review Letters that year, the theory provided an elegant, unified explanation for the fractional quantum Hall effect. The precise sequences of fractions his theory predicted are now known as the Jain sequences.

From Rural Rajasthan to Global Recognition

Jain's path to the prize began far from the world's research centers. He grew up in Sambhar, a small village on the eastern margin of the Thar Desert in Rajasthan. At age 12, while visiting family in Kolkata, a tram collided with his family's car. His mother never regained consciousness, and Jain suffered critical injuries that resulted in a lifelong disability.

The revolutionary low-cost Jaipur Foot prosthetic, developed by Dr. P.K. Sethi and craftsman Ram Chandra Sharma, helped him walk again and continue his education. He earned a bachelor's degree from Maharaja College in Jaipur, a master's from IIT Kanpur, and a PhD from Stony Brook University in New York.

"Looking back, it is hard to believe how incredibly fortunate I have been," Jain said after receiving the prize. "Growing up in a poor village in India, traumatized by an accident that left me on crutches with a lifelong disability, I did not think I would ever walk again or attend college, let alone pursue my dream of becoming a physicist."

Why the Prize Matters

The Wolf Prize in Physics, awarded annually by the Wolf Foundation in Israel since 1978, is widely regarded as one of the most prestigious awards in the field. Twenty-seven previous recipients have subsequently received the Nobel Prize, making it a strong indicator of potential Nobel recognition.

Composite fermions have proven far more universal than Jain anticipated. Originally introduced to explain one specific phenomenon, they were later found to form metals, crystals, ferromagnets, superconductors, and other correlated states. Some of their quantum states give rise to excitations that carry a fraction of an electron's charge — properties now being explored as potential building blocks for quantum computing.

Building Physics in India

Beyond his research at Penn State, Jain was appointed in 2026 as the founding director of the Lodha Theoretical Physics Institute in Mumbai, India's first fully privately funded center dedicated to fundamental research in theoretical physics.

"I hope LTPI will help create an environment where young scientists can pursue ambitious ideas, collaborate with outstanding researchers from around the world, and engage with the deepest questions in physics," Jain said.

Two other scientists of Indian origin have received Wolf Prizes in other categories: Gurdev Singh Khush and Venkatesan Sundaresan in Agriculture. Conductor Zubin Mehta received the Wolf Prize in Music.

What's Next

Jain told Nature India that he is currently working on fractional statistics, paired states of composite fermions, and new quantum phenomena in superconductors under strong magnetic fields. He noted that artificial intelligence methods are opening doors to questions previously beyond reach.

For young Indian researchers, his advice is direct: "Pursue questions that genuinely excite you. Ambitious science is rarely easy, but the most important discoveries often come from those willing to explore paths that others overlook."
